title: Matrices: Meaning, Order and Types
summary: What a matrix is, how to state its order, and the common types of matrix.

p: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns, placed in brackets. Rows run across and columns run down. The number in row i and column j is written aᵢⱼ. In this book a matrix is written row by row, with a semicolon between rows: A = [1 2 3 ; 4 5 6] has two rows, (1 2 3) and (4 5 6).
In A, a₁₂ = 2 (row 1, column 2) and a₂₃ = 6 (row 2, column 3).
The order is m × n, where m is the number of rows and n the number of columns (rows first). A = [1 2 3 ; 4 5 6] is 2 × 3. [5 ; 3 ; 1] is 3 × 1. [5 3 −1 8] is 1 × 4.
Row matrix: only one row, for example [5 3 −1 8] (order 1 × 4). Column matrix: only one column, for example [5 ; 3 ; 1] (3 × 1).
Square matrix: rows = columns, for example [1 2 ; 3 4] (2 × 2).
Diagonal matrix: a square matrix with zeros everywhere except possibly on the main diagonal, for example [3 0 ; 0 7].
Identity (unit) matrix I: a diagonal matrix with 1s on the diagonal, for example [1 0 ; 0 1]. For any matrix A, AI = IA = A.
Zero (null) matrix: every element is 0.
Scalar matrix: a diagonal matrix with equal diagonal elements, for example [5 0 ; 0 5].
Upper triangular: a square matrix with zeros below the main diagonal, for example [1 2 ; 0 3]. Lower triangular: zeros above the main diagonal, for example [1 0 ; 2 3].
Two matrices are equal if they have the same order and equal corresponding elements. If [x + 1 3 ; 2 y − 2] = [4 3 ; 2 5], then x + 1 = 4 and y − 2 = 5, so x = 3 and y = 7.

title: Matrix Operations: Addition, Scalar Multiplication and Multiplication
summary: How to add and subtract matrices, multiply by a number, and multiply two matrices, with the rule for when it is possible.

p: Matrices can be added or subtracted only if they have the same order. Add or subtract the corresponding elements. Let A = [1 2 ; 3 4] and B = [3 1 ; 2 5]. A + B = [4 3 ; 5 9]. A − B = [−2 1 ; 1 −1]. A + B = B + A, and A + O = A.
Multiply every element by the number. 3A = [3 6 ; 9 12]. −2[1 5 ; 0 3] = [−2 −10 ; 0 −6].

A (order m × n) times B (order p × q) is possible only if n = p (the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B). The product has order m × q. Each element of AB is found by multiplying a row of A by a column of B and adding.
Properties: (AB)C = A(BC); A(B + C) = AB + AC; AI = IA = A.

title: Transpose and Determinants
summary: The transpose of a matrix, and how to find the determinant of a 2 × 2 and a 3 × 3 matrix.

p: The transpose Aᵀ is found by interchanging rows and columns. If A = [1 2 3 ; 4 5 6], then Aᵀ = [1 4 ; 2 5 ; 3 6]. A 2 × 3 matrix has a 3 × 2 transpose. Properties: (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A; (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ; (kA)ᵀ = kAᵀ; (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ (the order is reversed). A matrix with A = Aᵀ is symmetric, for example [3 4 ; 4 6].

For A = [a b ; c d], |A| = ad − bc. Example: [3 2 ; 1 4] has determinant 3 × 4 − 2 × 1 = 10. [5 −2 ; 3 1] has determinant 5 × 1 − (−2)(3) = 11. [2 4 ; 1 2] has determinant 4 − 4 = 0: it is singular (it has no inverse).
For A = [a b c ; d e f ; g h i], expand along the first row: |A| = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg). Notice the minus sign before b.
Example 2. [1 2 3 ; 4 5 6 ; 7 8 9]: |A| = 1(45 − 48) − 2(36 − 42) + 3(32 − 35) = −3 + 12 − 9 = 0. The rows are dependent, so the matrix is singular.
Another way is the rule of Sarrus: copy the first two columns to the right, add the three downward diagonals and subtract the three upward diagonals.

If a row or column is all zeros, |A| = 0. If two rows (or columns) are identical, |A| = 0. |AB| = |A||B|. Interchanging two rows changes the sign of the determinant. For an n × n matrix, |kA| = kⁿ|A|.

title: Inverse of a 2 × 2 Matrix and Simultaneous Equations
summary: How to find the inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix and use it to solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations.

p: The inverse A⁻¹ of a square matrix A satisfies AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I. It exists only if |A| ≠ 0.
For A = [a b ; c d]: A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc)) × [d −b ; −c a]. Steps: find the determinant; swap a and d; change the signs of b and c; divide by the determinant.
Write the equations as AX = B. Then X = A⁻¹B.

If the determinant is zero the equations either have no solution or have infinitely many. Example: 2x + 4y = 6 and x + 2y = 5 have the matrix [2 4 ; 1 2] with determinant 0, and the equations contradict each other (the second gives 2x + 4y = 10).

activity: Find the inverse of [3 1 ; 5 2] ([2 −1 ; −5 3]) and use it to solve 3x + y = 5 and 5x + 2y = 9 (x = 1, y = 2).

title: Simultaneous Linear and Quadratic Equations
summary: Solving a linear and a quadratic equation together by substitution, including cases with surd answers.

p: A linear equation is y = mx + c: a straight line. A quadratic equation is y = ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 0): a parabola, which opens up if a > 0 and down if a < 0. To solve them together, substitute the linear equation into the quadratic one.

y = x + 2 and y = x² − 4. Substitute: x + 2 = x² − 4, so x² − x − 6 = 0, (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 3 or x = −2. Then y = 5 or y = 0. Solutions: (3, 5) and (−2, 0). Check (3, 5): 3 + 2 = 5 and 9 − 4 = 5.

y = 2x − 1 and y = x² + x − 5. 2x − 1 = x² + x − 5, so x² − x − 4 = 0. By the formula, x = (1 ± √17)/2, that is x ≈ 2.56 or x ≈ −1.56. Then y = 2x − 1 gives y ≈ 4.12 or y ≈ −4.12. Solutions: (2.56, 4.12) and (−1.56, −4.12).
x + y = 5 and x² + y² = 13. y = 5 − x, so x² + (5 − x)² = 13, 2x² − 10x + 25 = 13, x² − 5x + 6 = 0. x = 2 or 3. Solutions (2, 3) and (3, 2).

After substitution, the discriminant of the quadratic decides. If b² − 4ac > 0 the line cuts the curve at two points. If it is 0 the line is a tangent (one solution). If it is negative the line misses the curve (no real solution).

activity: Solve y = x + 1 and y = x² − 5 (x² − x − 6 = 0, so (3, 4) and (−2, −1)). Solve x − y = 2 and x² + y² = 20 (y = x − 2: 2x² − 4x − 16 = 0, x² − 2x − 8 = 0, so (4, 2) and (−2, −4)).

title: Graphical Solutions and Word Problems
summary: Solving a line and a curve together by graph, counting solutions, and word problems that lead to quadratic equations.

p: Draw both graphs on the same axes and read the coordinates of the points where they cross. Example: y = x + 1 and y = x² − 2x. Table for the curve: x = −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 gives y = 3, 0, −1, 0, 3, 8. The line crosses the curve near (−0.3, 0.7) and (3.3, 4.3). (By algebra: x² − 3x − 1 = 0, so x = (3 ± √13)/2 = 3.30 or −0.30.)

Number of solutions: two crossing points mean two solutions. A tangent touches at one point (a repeated root). A line that does not touch the curve means no real solution. Example: y = 2x − 1 and y = x² give x² − 2x + 1 = 0, so x = 1 twice: the line is a tangent at (1, 1). But y = 2x − 2 and y = x² give x² − 2x + 2 = 0, with discriminant −4: no solution.
The sum of two numbers is 10 and their product is 21. x + y = 10 and xy = 21. x(10 − x) = 21, x² − 10x + 21 = 0, (x − 3)(x − 7) = 0. The numbers are 3 and 7.

A rectangular field has length 5 m more than its width, and its area is 84 m². x(x + 5) = 84, x² + 5x − 84 = 0, (x + 12)(x − 7) = 0. The width is 7 m (reject −12) and the length is 12 m. Check: 7 × 12 = 84.

An investor buys (100 − x) shares at ₦x each and spends ₦2 400. x(100 − x) = 2 400, x² − 100x + 2 400 = 0, (x − 40)(x − 60) = 0. So the price is ₦40 and the number of shares is 60, or the price is ₦60 and the number of shares is 40. Both answers fit the information given.

title: Spheres and Hemispheres: Surface Area and Volume
summary: The formulas for the surface area and volume of a sphere and a hemisphere, with worked examples including the reverse problem of finding the radius.

p: A sphere is a perfectly round solid: every point on its surface is the same distance (the radius r) from the centre. Examples: a football, a globe, an orange and a marble. The diameter is d = 2r.
Surface area of a sphere = 4πr². (It is exactly 4 times the area of a circle with the same radius.) Volume of a sphere = (4/3)πr³.
1. Radius 7 cm. Surface area = 4 × (22/7) × 49 = 616 cm².
2. A balloon of radius 14 cm: surface area = 4 × (22/7) × 196 = 2 464 cm².
3. The surface area is 1 386 cm². Find the radius. 4 × (22/7) r² = 1 386, so r² = 1 386 × 7/88 = 110.25 and r = 10.5 cm.
6. A spherical tank of radius 1.5 m (π = 3.142): volume = (4/3)(3.142)(3.375) = 14.14 m³ = 14 140 litres (1 m³ = 1 000 litres).
Curved surface area = 2πr². Total surface area (with the flat circular face) = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr². Volume = (2/3)πr³.
Example. A hemispherical bowl of radius 7 cm: curved area = 2 × (22/7) × 49 = 308 cm²; total area = 462 cm²; volume = (2/3)(22/7)(343) = 718.67 cm³, about 0.72 litre.
Volume stays the same when a solid is melted and recast. A sphere of radius 6 cm is melted into small spheres of radius 2 cm. Number = (4/3)π(6)³ ÷ (4/3)π(2)³ = (6/2)³ = 27 small spheres.

activity: Find the surface area (1 386 cm²) and volume (4 851 cm³) of a sphere of radius 10.5 cm. A hemisphere has radius 14 cm; find its curved surface area (1 232 cm²) and volume (5 749.3 cm³).

title: Latitude and Longitude
summary: The geography of the globe: poles, equator, great and small circles, latitude and longitude, and the radius and length of a parallel of latitude.

p: The Earth is nearly a sphere. It spins about an axis through the North Pole and the South Pole. The equator is the circle halfway between the poles. A great circle is a circle on the sphere whose centre is the centre of the sphere (the equator and all meridians are great circles). A small circle is any other circle on the sphere, such as a parallel of latitude (other than the equator).

Latitude measures how far a place is north or south of the equator, as an angle at the centre of the Earth, from 0° at the equator to 90° at the poles (for example 6.5°N). Lines of latitude are called parallels. They are small circles, except the equator. Important latitudes: the equator 0°, the Tropic of Cancer 23.5°N, the Tropic of Capricorn 23.5°S.

Longitude measures how far a place is east or west of the prime meridian (the meridian through Greenwich, 0°), from 0° to 180°. Lines of longitude are called meridians and join the two poles. Each meridian is half of a great circle. The 180° meridian is roughly the International Date Line. A place is given as (latitude, longitude), for example Lagos is about (6.5°N, 3.4°E) and Abuja is about (9°N, 7.5°E).

sections.h: Radius of a parallel of latitude
p: The radius of the parallel of latitude θ is r = R cos θ, where R is the radius of the Earth (about 6 400 km in these notes). At the equator (θ = 0°) r = R. At the poles (θ = 90°) r = 0.

img.alt: A cross-section of the Earth showing the equator, the polar axis and a point P at latitude theta, with the radius of the parallel marked r equals R cos theta

p: 1. Latitude 60°N: r = 6 400 × cos 60° = 3 200 km. Length of the parallel = 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 3 200 = 20 114.29 km.
3. Latitude 30°S: r = 6 400 × cos 30° = 5 542.56 km. Length of the parallel = 2 × (22/7) × 5 542.56 = 34 838.96 km. (Some printed notes give 34 805.83 km; that is not correct for these values.)
4. A parallel has radius 3 200 km. Then cos θ = 3 200/6 400 = 0.5, so θ = 60° (60°N or 60°S).
